Learning Objectives
Review the epidemiology and etiology of benign tumors of fatty tissue.
Explain the evaluation, imaging, pathology, and management of lipoma and histologic variants
of lipoma.
Describe the presentation and diagnosis of benign vascular neoplasms and malformations.
List indications for the management of benign vascular neoplasms and recurrence.
Review the epidemiology and etiology of benign tumors of neural origin.
Describe the evaluation, imaging, pathology, and management of schwannomas,
schwannomatosis, neurofibromas, perineuromas, nerve sheath myxomas, traumatic
neuromas, and Morton neuromas.

Introduction

Introduction
Malignant soft-tissue sarcomas are extremely rare, with an estimated 13,000 new soft-
tissue sarcomas predicted to occur in the United States in 2021.1 Soft-tissue sarcomas
are very rare; however, benign soft-tissue tumors outnumber soft-tissue sarcomas by a
factor of at least 100. Many benign soft-tissue masses are not true neoplasms but are
pseudotumors caused by sequelae of trauma, cystic masses, or vascular conditions. This
lesson reviews the most common benign soft-tissue masses categorized by tissue type
or whether they are true neoplasms.
Tumors of Fatty Tissue
Lipoma
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
2/47

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Lipomas are benign neoplasms consisting of mature adipose tissue.
Epidemiology
Most common mesenchymal neoplasm (benign and malignant)
Slightly more common in men than women
Highest incidence in middle age (40 to 60 years)
No difference in incidence with race
Slightly higher incidence in sedentary individuals
Etiology/Risk Factors
 Most lipomas are associated with chromosomal abnormalities.
Common genes involved are HMGA1 and LPP. 2
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical Presentation
Most patients present with a painless superficial soft-tissue mass.
If patients have pain, it likely is from another source.
Deep lipomas may not be discretely palpable but may present as generalized swelling or
asymmetry.
Slow growing
Will increase in size initially then plateau
Physical Examination
Can be superficial or deep to the fascia (superficial much more common)
Superficial lipomas are soft and rubbery with palpation.
Often mobile
Nontender
Truncal locations (upper back, abdomen, posterior neck) are more common than extremity
locations.
Proximal extremity location is more common than distal extremity location.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
3/47

Approximately 5% to 10% of patients have multiple lipomas.
Imaging Studies
MRI with contrast is the best imaging modality.
Homogenous mass that is isointense to normal subcutaneous fat on all sequences; does not
enhance (Figure 1).
The mass may have some septations or heterogeneity from calcifications or vascularity.
Should not have internal nodularity or considerable enhancement (concerning features for a
higher grade liposarcoma)
Cannot reliably differentiate between lipoma and atypical lipomatous tumor 3
CT: for patients with considerable claustrophobia or obtained for another reason (ie, chest or
abdominal/pelvic CT)
Homogenous mass that has a radiodensity identical to normal subcutaneous fat
Plain radiography: not very sensitive for detecting or diagnosing lipomas
May reveal a soft-tissue shadow
Underlying cortical erosion is more concerning for malignancy.
Figure 1 MRIs of a right medial thigh show that lipomas appear isometric to subcutaneous fat on
all sequences. Lipomas appear bright on T1-weighted MRI (A), appear dark on T2-weighted MRI
(B), and show no enhancement on T1-weighted MRI with contrast (C). (Courtesy of Lee Jae Morse,
MD, Oakland, CA.)
Pathology
Gross pathology (Figure 2)
Superficial lipomas (2 to 8 cm) generally are smaller than deep lipomas. (thigh and buttock
lipomas may be as large as 25 cm)
Most superficial lipomas are round or oval.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
4/47

Deep lipomas grow in a centripetal pattern and are often multi-lobulated because they grow
in locations within the compartment with the least resistance.
Whitish-yellow and usually surrounded by a well-defined capsule
Some deep intramuscular lipomas may interdigitate within muscle fibers, making complete
excision more difficult.
Figure 2 Photograph shows a well-encapsulated lipomatous mass. Lipoma usually is soft with
palpation. The mass is mobile if subcutaneous, and often is firmer and nonmobile if
intramuscular. (Courtesy of Lee Jae Morse, MD, Oakland, CA.)
Histology
Mature adipocytes with large lipid droplets and bland basophilic nuclei are pushed to the side,
often representing a signet ring.
On low-power histologic images, the cells form an interlocking pattern with chicken wire
appearance (Figure 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
5/47

Figure 3 Histologic image of a lipoma shows a chicken-wire appearance of cells (magnification
×20). (Reproduced from McGarry SV: Lipoma and other benign lipomatous tumors, in Biermann
JS, Siegel GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 271-277.)
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Observation only
No surveillance imaging studies are necessary unless a substantial change in size or character
(ie, mass shifts from very soft to firm or hard) occurs.
Excision would cause considerable morbidity or a high risk of complications
If diagnosis is questionable, the patient should be referred to an orthopaedic oncologist.
Surgical Management
Indications
Almost always elective
Cosmetic concerns
Patient preference—Although lipomas are benign, patients often are nervous about leaving a
tumor in their bodies.
Large size
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
6/47

Pain: uncommon; however, lipomas in the forearm or very large lipomas in other areas may
cause compression and discomfort. 
Nerve compression: extremely unusual for lipoma to result in symptomatic nerve
compression; however, large lipomas in the popliteal fossa or within the greater sciatic notch
may cause symptoms.
Technique
Marginal excision
Intralesional if a portion is interdigitated within muscle fibers; avoid resecting large portions of
normal muscle.
Place drain if appropriate to close the dead space.
Lipomatosis
Term encompassing many syndromes that cause diffuse excessive deposition of lipomatous
tissue within the body.
Madelung disease: symmetric accumulation of fat in the neck and upper shoulder region
(horse collar); not to be confused with Madelung deformity of the wrist.
Diffuse lipomatosis: asymmetric accumulation of fat in an extremity or truncal area
Steroid lipomatosis
Pelvic lipomatosis: excessive accumulation of fat around the rectum and bladder
Lipoma Arborescens
Subsynovial lipomatous villous projections, most commonly in the knee
MRI findings described as tree-like (arborescens) projections of fat arising from the synovium
Projections have fat signal (appear bright on T1-weighted images, dark on T2-weighted
images and suppress on fat-suppression images).
Lipoma is a misnomer because lipoma arborescens is not a true neoplasm.
Etiology is unknown but usually is related to other intra-articular pathology.
Clinically presents as effusion, pain, catching
Treatment for symptomatic patients is open or arthroscopic synovectomy.
Lipoblastoma
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
7/47

Benign tumor composed of immature adipose cells (lipoblasts)
Occurs in infants and very young children (usually younger than 5 years) 4
More common in males than in females
Most often within the subcutaneous tissues
May have cystic or myxoid component
Fluorescence in situ hybridization studies for PLAG1 gene rearrangement (8q11-13) 5
Management is marginal excision.
Low local recurrence risk unless incompletely excised
Diffuse type has associated with a much higher recurrence risk because of inability to
perform complete excision.
Spindle Cell/Pleomorphic Lipoma
Benign lipomatous mass composed of lipocytes and spindle cells, with a myxoid stroma
Most commonly occurs in the posterior shoulder and upper back (shawl area)
Older patients (aged 50 to 60 years)
Male predominance
Deletion on 13q in most spindle cell lipomas 6
Lack RB1 gene
Manage via marginal excision.
Hibernoma
Benign lipomatous mass composed of brown fat and usually vascular
Can appear more concerning on MRI
80% are subcutaneous.
Low recurrence
Manage via marginal excision
Neural Fibrolipoma
Lipomatous infiltration of peripheral nerves
Typically observed in young patients (usually <30 years)
Most common location is the volar surface of the upper extremities.
Can cause nerve compressive symptoms
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
8/47

Manage in symptomatic patients via marginal excision (avoid injuring nerve given the benign
nature of the lesion).
Myolipoma
Lipomatous mass intermixed with mature smooth muscle cells
Typically observed in middle-aged adults
Superficial masses usually are smaller than 5 cm.
Subfascial masses may become quite large (10 to 15 cm).
Histology shows eosinophilic smooth muscle cells within normal-appearing adipocytes.
Manage in symptomatic patients via marginal excision.
Angiolipoma
Small lipomatous masses with large vascular infiltration
Common location is the volar forearm.
Often multiple
Usually superficial (<2 cm)
May be painful and tender
Histology shows mature adipocytes with vascular infiltration, with fibrin thrombi within the
vascular channels.
Manage in symptomatic patients via marginal resection.
Chondroid Lipoma
Lipomatous mass with a prominence of chondroid matrix
Much more common in females
Often painless
Histology shows mature adipocytes and small round cells with granular cytoplasm within a
chondroid matrix.
Fusion oncogene C11 or f95-MKL2 resulting from t (11;16) (q13; p13) 6,7
Manage in symptomatic patients via marginal excision.
Anisometric Cell/Dysplastic Lipoma
Lipomatous mass with areas of fat necrosis and fibrous/fibromyxoid tissue 8
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
9/47

Adipocytes are variable in size and have atypia.
Manage in symptomatic patients via marginal excision.
Vascular Soft-Tissue Lesions
Introduction

Introduction
Benign vascular anomalies may be neoplastic or aberrant developmental growths. In
either case, adolescent patients present with a painful mass. The mass typically is larger
and more symptomatic during/after exercise, consistent with increased blood flow.
Observation usually is adequate, with management reserved for symptomatic lesions.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Vascular Neoplasms
Hemangioma
Infantile cutaneous variant characterized by proliferating phase followed by involuting phase
Because of spontaneous involution, observation is recommended.
If hemangioma persists, laser therapy, steroids, or propranolol may be considered.
Surgical management is considered a last treatment option.
Hemangioendothelioma
Uncertain biologic behavior; diagnosis is made via pathology.
Approximately 15% to 25% may exhibit aggressive or malignant behavior.
Consequently, recommended management is wide resection.
Papillary Endothelial Hyperplasia (Masson Tumor)
Excessive endothelial proliferation within vessels
Diagnosed after resection; clinically indistinguishable from other vascular lesions.
Recurrence after resection is rare.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
10/47

Developmental Vascular Malformations

Developmental Vascular Malformations
Patients (usually in their adolescent years) often present with the main symptom of pain
that may be worse with activity or limb dependency. Developmental vascular
malformations may be cutaneous, subcutaneous, or intramuscular in location. Intra-
articular locations may be associated with hemarthrosis.
Low-Flow (Venous, Capillary) Neoplasms
Most common form, also referred to as intramuscular hemangioma
May be hormonally responsive (eg, may enlarge during pregnancy)
High-Flow (Arteriovenous) Neoplasms
Less common than venous
Mass may be pulsatile.
Associated Syndromes
Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome (venous and lymphatic malformations, limb overgrowth)
Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (giant hemangioma, thrombocytopenia, consumption
coagulopathy)
Maffucci syndrome (cutaneous and visceral vascular malformations, multiple enchondromas)
Parkes Weber syndrome (venous and lymphatic malformations, limb overgrowth)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Pain in the adolescent years is the typical patient presentation (if not discovered incidentally)
for any of these vascular lesions.
MRI with and without contrast is the preferred imaging modality for evaluation.
Ultrasonography also may be used to evaluate flow and monitor for changes over time.
Pathologic evaluation helps distinguish the different lesions; however, all of the lesions are
managed in the same manner if patients are symptomatic.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
11/47

Management
If a patient has minimal symptoms, observation is reasonable.
Nonsurgical management consists of gentle compressive wraps and elevation to reduce
swelling and associated symptoms.
Sclerotherapy or embolization may be considered for symptomatic lesions with definable
feeding vessels.
Surgical resection may be considered; local recurrence is observed in 19% to 38% of patients.
Tumors of Neural Tissue
Schwannoma (Neurilemmoma)
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Benign, well-encapsulated mass arising from Schwann cells
Epidemiology
Occur in patients aged 30 to 60 years
No gender predilection
Etiology/Risk Factors
Sporadic and heritable subtypes
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical Presentation
Occurs at locations at which nerve fibers exist, classically on flexor surface of the extremities,
head, and neck
Physical Examination
Mass may be tender and painful with radiating pain in the affected nerve distribution (often
positive Tinel sign).
Imaging Studies
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
12/47

MRI with contrast is best imaging modality (Figure 4).
Often ovoid or fusiform mass
String/tail sign
Figure 4 Images of a thigh with a posterior, distal large schwannoma involving the sciatic nerve.
T1-weighted axial (A) and sagittal (B) MRIs with contrast show the string/tail sign representing the
associated nerve. C, Clinical photograph of the gross specimen shows a white oval/fusiform mass.
(Courtesy of Lee Jae Morse, MD, Oakland, CA.)
Pathology
Well encapsulated; usually eccentric on the nerve but may be within the nerve.
Two distinct histologic regions
Antoni A: highly ordered Schwann cells arranged in linear arrays or sheets (Figure 5)
Verocay bodies: stacked arrangements of elongated palisading nuclei (Figure 6)
Antoni B: loosely arranged and less cellular region; has extracellular mucin.
Stains positive for S100
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
13/47

Figure 5 Low-power histologic image shows a schwannoma, which is characterized by alternating
compact Antoni type A tissues (left) and loose Antoni type B tissues (right; hematoxylin-eosin,
magnification ×100). (Reproduced from Bozorgnia S: Benign neural tumors, in Biermann JS, Siegel
GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 279-291.)
Figure 6 High-power histologic image of a schwannoma shows Verocay bodies, which are
composed of palisaded arrays of nuclei separated by vaguely fibrillary collections of cell
processes (hematoxylin-eosin, magnification ×200). (Reproduced from Bozorgnia S: Benign neural
tumors, in Biermann JS, Siegel GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed
4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 279-291.)
Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
14/47

Nonsurgical Management
Observation for asymptomatic masses
Surgical Management
Marginal excision for symptomatic schwannomas
Eccentric schwannomas usually are easily separable from nerve fibers.
If the schwannoma is within the motor nerve itself, the surgeon can use neuromonitoring or a
nerve stimulator to identify fibers. An incision is made in bare area to preserve function.
Outcomes
Goal is to preserve function because risk of recurrence is minimal and if residual tumor
remains, progression is unlikely.
Malignant transformation is extremely rare in patients with solitary schwannomas.
Schwannomatosis (Multiple Schwannomas)
Cannot have neurofibromatosis type 2
Approximately 79% of patients have spine tumors, necessitating MRI with contrast of the
entire spine.9
Neurofibroma
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Benign nerve sheath tumor composed of Schwann cells and fibroblasts within collagen and a
myxoid stroma
Epidemiology
Occurs in patients aged 30 years
No gender predilection
Etiology/Risk Factors
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
15/47

Neurofibromin 1 gene mutation (neurofibromatosis type 1 [NF1])
10% related to NF1 (multiple neurofibromas)
Diagnosis criteria for NF1 (at least two of the six findings)
Six or more café au lait spots 5 mm or larger in diameter in prepubertal patients or 15 mm or
larger in adults
More than two neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma
Freckling of axillary or inguinal areas
More than two Lisch nodules of the iris
First-degree relative with NF1
Optic glioma
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical Presentation
Can occur in any peripheral nerve, skin, soft tissue, and bone
Most lesions are solitary.
Physical Examination
Firm mass
May be tender to palpation
Imaging Studies
Neurofibromas often are central to the nerve, whereas schwannomas tend to be eccentric to
the nerve (Figure 7).
Target sign: bright signal periphery surrounding a relatively low signal intensity center (Figure
8).

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
16/47

Figure 7 Schematic drawings show the eccentric position of a schwannoma (A) in relation to the
parent nerve and the central location of a neurofibroma (B). (Reproduced from Bozorgnia S:
Benign neural tumors, in Biermann JS, Siegel GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update:
Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021,
pp 279-291.)
Figure 8 Axial T2-weighted MRI of the left upper arm with a neurofibroma shows the target sign
(arrow), in which a central low signal intensity and a peripheral high signal intensity are observed.
(Reproduced from Bozorgnia S: Benign neural tumors, in Biermann JS, Siegel GW, eds:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 279-291.)
Pathology
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
17/47

Firm, gray-white mass
Not encapsulated
Contains Schwann cells and fibroblasts in wavy bundles (Figure 9)
Myxoid stroma
Figure 9 Histologic images of a neurofibroma. A, Low-power image) shows the characteristic low
cellularity and bands of collagen (hematoxylin-eosin, magnification ×100). B, High-power image
shows the waviness of collagen (occasionally described as the shredded carrot appearance) and
tumor cell nuclei (hematoxylin-eosin, magnification ×400). (Reproduced from Bozorgnia S: Benign
neural tumors, in Biermann JS, Siegel GW, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Musculoskeletal
Tumors, ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 279-291.)
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Asymptomatic stable masses may be managed via observation.
Neurofibroma may be intimate with the nerve, necessitating resection of the nerve with the
mass; if located on a major functional nerve, observation may be permitted.
Biopsy masses that have been stable but then start growing.
Surgical Management
Treat symptomatic lesions with marginal excision.
Outcomes
10% to 13% risk of malignant transformation with NF110
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
18/47

Perineuroma
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Benign soft-tissue mass composed of perineurial cells
Two types
Soft-tissue perineuroma (storiform perineurial fibroma)
Painless mass not associated with a nerve on the trunk or extremity
Intraneural perineuroma
Associated with a nerve and may cause sensorimotor dysfunction
Epidemiology
Occurs at any age
Occurs in women more than men
Management
Excision is curative with low recurrence rate.
Nerve Sheath Myxoma
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Benign tumor of the dermis
Epidemiology
Affects patients of all ages, with a peak occurring in individuals in their thirties
No gender predilection
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical Presentation
Approximately 85% found in the extremities
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
19/47

Common in the fingers or knee in the infrapatellar region
Pathology
Histology shows highly myxoid tumor with some axons (rare); dense fibrous capsule
Stains positive for S100
Management
Manage via wide excision if not considerably morbid because of high local recurrence rate.
Traumatic Neuroma
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Not a neoplasm
Etiology/Risk Factors
Occurs after laceration, amputation, or blunt impact
After laceration, nerve undergoes Wallerian degeneration.
Growth factors stimulate nerve regrowth; however, the lesion is disorganized nerve fascicles
that form a neuroma.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical Presentation
Presents as painful and tender nodule
Physical Examination
May have positive Tinel sign
Pathology
Histologically, neuroma is composed of normal components of fascicle.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
20/47

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Opioids, anticonvulsant agents, antidepressants, N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonists,
local anesthetic agents, and calcitonin11
Surgical Management
Targeted nerve implantation/targeted muscle reinnervation12
Postamputation procedure
Excise neuroma
Transect an adjacent motor nerve
Anastomose affected nerve to adjacent motor nerve
Manage via excision of neuroma; pull the nerve distally and transect as proximal as possible so
the nerve retracts into muscle or soft tissue, which decreases pressure on the nerve ending
that can stimulate nerve regrowth. Alternative procedures that involve implanting the nerve
ending into muscle also have been successful.
Morton Neuroma
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Compressive neuropathy of common digital nerve of the foot
Most common in the second and third intermetatarsal spaces
Epidemiology
Occurs in individuals in their twenties
Occurs in females more than males
Etiology/Risk Factors
Exacerbated with narrow closed-toe shoes
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical Presentation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
21/47

Present with tenderness, burning, or numbness in the forefoot
Physical Examination
Neuroma may be palpable.
Positive web-space compression test
Imaging Studies
Weight-bearing radiographs are useful to evaluate for underlying arthritis or lesions.
Ultrasonography: ovoid hypoechoic signal in the intermetatarsal space
MRI usually is not indicated but typically will show neuroma or other lesions; can confirm
examination findings
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Wide-toe shoes (avoid high-heeled shoes), metatarsal pads, steroid injections
Steroid injection can be used as a diagnostic tool. Evidence for long-term relief is equivocal.
Surgical Management
Initial management is nonsurgical.
Dorsal neurectomy: most common
Decompression by releasing the transverse metatarsal ligament
Intramuscular Myxoma
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
A benign, nonaggressive myxomatous soft-tissue tumor
Epidemiology
Occurs in adults aged 40 to 70 years
Very rare in young adults13
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
22/47

Male-to-female ratio of 1:2
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical Presentation
Usually presents as a painless mass
Pain/tenderness in approximately 20% of patients
Large lesions may cause numbness or paresthesias because of mass effect.
Usually solitary
Most commonly located in the thigh, buttocks, shoulder, or upper arm
Often close to neurovascular structures

Clinical Presentation
Multiple intramuscular myxomas are associated with fibrous dysplasia (Mazabraud
syndrome). In Mazabraud syndrome, fibrous dysplasia develops at a young age, and the
myxomas occur later in the same general anatomic area, typically years later.
Imaging Studies
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI appearance is homogeneous.
Low signal intensity (lower than muscle) on T1-weighted images, high signal intensity on T2-
weighted images (Figure 10, A and B)
Located within the muscle groups; usually 5 to 10 cm in size.
Pathology
Gross appearance: lobular and gelatinous with cyst-like spaces (Figure 10, C)
Histology
Minimal cellularity with cells suspended in abundant mucoid material (Figure 10, D)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:27 AM
AAOS | Benign Soft-Tissue Tumors and Reactive Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000543
23/47

Loose network of reticulin fibers
No atypia and only sparse vascularity
Cellular myxoma has increased cellularity and may be mistaken for a malignant myxoid
neoplasm.
Figure 10 Images of intramuscular myxoma. Axial T1-weighted (A) and T2-weighted (B) MRIs of
the right knee of a 58-year-old woman show a soft-tissue mass along the posteromedial aspect of
the vastus medialis consistent with an intramuscular myxoma. The mass has a lower signal
intensity than muscle on the T1-weighted image and appears bright on the T2-weighted image. C,
Photograph shows the gross appearance of a bisected intramuscular myxoma. Note the white,
gelatinous surface. D, Histologic image of an intramuscular myxoma shows a paucicellular lesion
with extensive reticulin fibers and a mucoid stroma (hematoxylin-eosin). (Reproduced from

Introduction
The two most common synovial proliferative disorders are tenosynovial giant cell tumor
(previously known as pigmented villonodular synovitis) and synovial chondromatosis.
Because both disorders involve joints (most commonly the knee), mechanical symptoms
and joint effusions are reported, and surgical synovectomy remains the standard of care
for these conditions.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Proliferative disease of intra-articular and periarticular synovium
Spectrum of presentations
Localized/nodular (single, well-defined mass; self-limiting, classically located on the deep
surface of the patellar tendon)
Diffuse (areas of disease in more than one location throughout the joint; often progressive,
can erode into bone)
Extra-articular
All forms are histologically identical.
Overexpression of CSF-1 (t(1;2) translocation) creates autocrine/paracrine loop with
macrophages.

Typically affects females more than males, between the ages of 30 and 50 years
Clinical history of intermittent but progressive pain and swelling of joint
Nodular form may present as mechanical symptoms.
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for diagnosis (assess for hemosiderin deposits).

Surgical Resection

Etiology
The exact pathophysiology of myositis ossificans has yet to be fully elucidated. The
inflammatory cascade that follows muscle injury leads to a release of cytokines,
including bone morphogenetic proteins 2 and 4. These chemicals further trigger
reactions within the skeletal muscle vascular endothelial cells to transform into
osteoblasts or chondroblasts.34

Myositis ossificans is a self-limiting process.
The natural history of myositis ossificans can be viewed as three analogous processes
occurring clinically, radiologically, and histopathologically34 (Table 1).
The size of the mass often decreases after 1 year.
